assessmentSummary.identity: A progressive run-in followed by a 10-meter maximal-velocity zone and a controlled run-out.
currentCardFindings: The card is materially the same exercise as Flying 10 and differs primarily in naming and measurement unit.
The generic description does not define build-in distance, timing, dosage, run-out, or a quality stop rule.
Controlled taxonomy, anatomy, constraints, load, fatigue, and complete difficulty fields are empty.
assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Resolve this card to the Flying 10 canonical identity after human identity review. Preserve Flying 10m Sprint as an alias and store the metric fly-zone length in dosage.

currentCardSnapshot.description: Flying 10m Sprint is a max velocity & rhythm exercise for speed, sprinting, and quick-release athletes. It emphasizes upright sprint cycle, front side mechanics, elastic foot contact while keeping the session intent aligned with the Vortex phase sequence.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Training and Development of Elite Sprint Performance: an Integration of Scientific and Best Practice Literature
claims: Flying sprints use a progressive run-in to reach high velocity before a short maximal-velocity zone.
Flying 10m Sprint must separate run-in distance, measured fly-zone distance, intent, and timing method from its stable exercise identity.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Training and Development of Elite Sprint Performance: an Integration of Scientific and Best Practice Literature
claims: Acceleration, maximal velocity, and speed endurance are related but distinct sprint-training qualities.
Flying 10m Sprint belongs to upright high-speed locomotion; dense repeated-sprint conditioning requires a separate delivery profile.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Influence of Weekly Sprint Volume and Maximal Velocity Exposures on Eccentric Hamstring Strength in Professional Football Players
claims: Maximal-velocity exposures impose meaningful eccentric hamstring demand in addition to whole-lower-limb and trunk demands.
The card should identify bilateral hip, knee, and ankle actions, posterior-chain loading, calf-foot stiffness demand, and trunk-pelvis control.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Training and Development of Elite Sprint Performance: an Integration of Scientific and Best Practice Literature
claims: Maximal running velocity depends on the interaction of step length, step rate, short contact time, force production, and coordinated upright sprint mechanics.
Coaching should preserve individual solutions and avoid forcing one universal limb position or artificially reaching for stride length.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Longitudinal Effects of Resisted and Assisted Sprint Training on Sprint Kinematics, Acceleration, and Maximum Velocity: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
claims: Unresisted flying, resisted, assisted, and combined sprint methods create materially different kinematic and force-velocity demands.
Exercise difficulty must score physical demand and technical complexity directly, including coordination, supervision, impact, and failure consequence; it must not use a skill-library level.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Influence of Weekly Sprint Volume and Maximal Velocity Exposures on Eccentric Hamstring Strength in Professional Football Players
claims: Weekly high-speed sprint exposure can measurably affect eccentric hamstring force capacity.
Flying 10m Sprint needs explicit high-speed distance, contact, neural-intent, posterior-chain stress, performance-drop, session-recovery, and weekly-exposure tracking.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Need for Speed—Improving Sprinting Performance in Football Players
claims: Flying and wicket drills require a suitable running surface, marked zones, progressive build-in, and a clear deceleration area.
Footwear, weather, lane separation, equipment placement, timing setup, run-out distance, and coach sightline are hard delivery constraints.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Training and Development of Elite Sprint Performance: an Integration of Scientific and Best Practice Literature
claims: Run-in and fly-zone length should match the athlete's ability to reach and briefly preserve maximal velocity.
Prescribe build-in distance, fly-zone distance, total high-speed distance, repetitions, intensity, inter-repetition recovery, and a performance-drop stop rule.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Need for Speed—Improving Sprinting Performance in Football Players
claims: The athlete should accelerate progressively into upright high-speed mechanics rather than attack the fly zone from a cold or abrupt start.
Use a small number of observable cues: build smoothly, run tall without leaning back, strike beneath the body, keep arm action coordinated, sprint through the zone, and decelerate gradually.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Influence of Weekly Sprint Volume and Maximal Velocity Exposures on Eccentric Hamstring Strength in Professional Football Players
claims: High-speed sprint load and recent exposure must be monitored rather than inferred from repetition count alone.
Stop for pain, hamstring or calf tightness, limping, stumble, unsafe surface or spacing, repeated overstriding, loss of upright control, or a persistent velocity or timing decline.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Training and Development of Elite Sprint Performance: an Integration of Scientific and Best Practice Literature
claims: Flying sprints are used to develop maximal velocity and should continue only while velocity and mechanics remain stable.
Flying 10m Sprint belongs early in a session after preparation and before fatigue-oriented work; rehabilitation, conditioning, and assisted-speed uses require separate contextual profiles.
Fly-in work isolates a short maximal-velocity action zone after an acceleration zone.
Athlete-facing support should show the zone layout, define a successful rep, limit the cue count, state the run-out expectation, and explain the stop signal.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Need for Speed—Improving Sprinting Performance in Football Players
claims: Coaches can use marked fly zones and timing to observe or monitor top-speed performance.
Coach support should include setup measurements, athlete-specific build-in choice, contact and posture observations, split consistency, spacing control, regression choices, and recovery decisions.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Training and Long-Term Athletic Development
claims: Speed work should be developmentally appropriate and follow movement competency, readiness, and progressive exposure.
Intent, run-in length, fly-zone length, timing pressure, cue complexity, wicket spacing, and total exposure can be scaled without assigning the exercise a skill level.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Longitudinal Effects of Resisted and Assisted Sprint Training on Sprint Kinematics, Acceleration, and Maximum Velocity: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
claims: Normal, resisted, assisted, and combined sprinting produce different training conditions and should not be collapsed into one undifferentiated card.
Fly-zone length is dosage, run-in style is usually a variant, and external assistance or resistance may require a distinct definition when it changes the primary stimulus and safety model.
